content: Bartonella Infections 1. Bartonella quintana Acute or chronic infections without endocarditis: The preferred treatment involves administering doxycycline at a dose of 200 mg orally once daily or 100 mg orally twice daily for 4 weeks, combined with gentamicin at 3 mg/kg intravenously once daily for the first 2 weeks. Endocarditis: The recommended regimen includes gentamicin at 3 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8 hours for 14 days, along with ceftriaxone at 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 6 weeks. Doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks may be added. 2. Bartonella elizabethae Endocarditis: The treatment mirrors that of Bartonella quintana endocarditis, with gentamicin at 3 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8 hours for 14 days and ceftriaxone at 2 g intravenously every 24 hours for 6 weeks. Doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks may also be included. 3. Bartonella bacilliformis Oroya fever: The preferred treatment is ciprofloxacin at 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days. For severe disease, ceftriaxone at 1 g intravenously daily for 14 days should be added. Verruga peruana: The first-line treatment is azithromycin at 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days. Alternative regimens include rifampin at 600 mg orally once daily for 14–21 days or ciprofloxacin at 500 mg orally twice daily for 7–10 days. 4. Bartonella henselae Cat scratch disease: No treatment is typically recommended for uncomplicated cases. However, if extensive lymphadenopathy is present: For pediatric patients: Azithromycin at 500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg orally once daily on days 2–5. For adults: Azithromycin at 1 g orally on day 1, followed by 500 mg orally daily for 4 days. Endocarditis: The preferred regimen includes gentamicin at 3 mg/kg/day intravenously every 8 hours for 14 days, combined with ceftriaxone at 2 g/day intravenously for 6 weeks. Doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for 6 weeks may be added. Retinitis: The recommended treatment is doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily, combined with rifampin at 300 mg orally twice daily for 4–6 weeks. Bacillary angiomatosis: First-line options include erythromycin at 500 mg orally four times daily for at least 2 months or doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for at least 2 months. Bacillary peliosis: Preferred regimens are erythromycin at 500 mg orally four times daily for at least 4 months or doxycycline at 100 mg orally twice daily for at least 4 months. Neurocysticercosis 1. Parenchymal Neurocysticercosis Single lesions: The preferred treatment is albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 3–8 days, combined with prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day orally four times daily for 8–10 days, followed by a taper. Multiple cysts: Albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 8–15 days is recommended, along with high-dose corticosteroids. Alternatively, praziquantel at 50 mg/kg/day orally in three divided doses can be combined with albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses. Cysticercal encephalitis: Antiparasitic therapy is contraindicated due to the risk of exacerbating inflammation and cerebral edema, which can lead to transtentorial herniation. Most cases improve with corticosteroid therapy. Calcified cysts: Parenchymal calcifications are a significant risk factor for recurrent seizures. Seizures should be managed with antiepileptic therapy. 2. Extraparenchymal Neurocysticercosis Subarachnoid cysts: Albendazole at 15 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 28 days is recommended, along with prednisone (up to 60 mg/day orally) or dexamethasone (up to 24 mg/day). Steroid therapy may require tapering or substitution with methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent for prolonged use. Giant cysts: These are typically associated with cerebral edema and mass effect, requiring management with high-dose corticosteroids, with or without mannitol. Intraventricular cysts: Emergency management involves cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion via ventriculostomy or ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. Residual hydrocephalus may be treated with endoscopic foraminotomy and third ventriculostomy, which can also facilitate cyst removal. Ocular cysticercosis: Surgical excision is indicated for intraocular cysts. Extraocular muscle involvement should be treated with albendazole and corticosteroids. Spinal cysticercosis: Treatment involves corticosteroids and antiparasitic drugs. Ectoparasites 1. Body Lice (Pediculus humanus corporis) Treatment involves improving personal hygiene, including regular (at least weekly) changes of clean clothes. Clothing, bedding, and towels should be laundered in hot water (≥130°F) and machine-dried on a hot cycle. Pediculicides, such as ivermectin lotion, are generally unnecessary if hygiene is maintained. 2. Head Lice (Pediculus humanus capitis) Preferred regimens: Permethrin 1% lotion applied to shampooed, dried hair for 10 minutes, with a repeat application in 9–10 days. Malathion 0.5% lotion applied to dry hair for 8–12 hours, followed by shampooing (two doses, 7–9 days apart). Alternative regimen: Ivermectin at 200 μg/kg orally as a single dose, repeated every 7 days for three doses. 3. Pubic Lice (Phthirus pubis) Preferred regimens: Permethrin 1% cream rinse applied to affected areas and washed off after 10 minutes. Pyrethrins with piperonyl butoxide applied to affected areas and washed off after 10 minutes. Alternative regimens: Malathion 0.5% lotion applied to affected areas and washed off after 8–12 hours. Ivermectin at 250 μg/kg orally, repeated in 2 weeks. 4. Myiasis No FDA-approved medications are available. Treatment involves occluding the punctum to prevent gas exchange (e.g., with petrolatum, nail polish, makeup cream, or bacon) and manually removing the larvae when they migrate. Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei) 1. Adults Preferred regimens: Permethrin 5% cream applied to the entire body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Ivermectin at 200 μg/kg orally once daily, repeated in 2 weeks. Alternative regimen: Lindane 1% lotion or cream applied in a thin layer to the entire body from the neck down and washed off after 8 hours. 2. Infants and Young Children Permethrin 5% cream applied to the entire body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Lindane is contraindicated in children under 10 years of age. 3. Crusted Scabies (Norwegian Scabies) Treatment involves a combination of topical scabicides (e.g., 5% benzyl benzoate or 5% permethrin cream applied daily for 7 days, then twice weekly until resolution) and oral ivermectin at 200 μg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9, and 15. Additional doses on days 22 and 29 may be required for severe cases. 4. Pregnant or Lactating Women Permethrin 5% cream applied to the entire body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours is the preferred treatment.
